transcript.answer_text:
We sang him more than we defined him.

To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. That was the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first.

In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. Every single thing they had been carrying forward finally arrived.

His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. That is what his rising meant to us - not only that he came back, but that the grave gives back its dead because he went in first and broke it open from the inside.

And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people. That was the name we called him most often. Not judge first, not king first - Physician. The one who exists for wounds, not the one scandalized by them.

We do not offer you a formula for this. We offer you what we sang.

Our own answer was a story. Addai the apostle came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. And that story, we must say honestly, is our cherished legend - written down late, not a document from the beginning.

King Abgar the Black lay sick in Edessa. He heard of Jesus and his healings from envoys returning through Jerusalem, and he wrote Jesus a letter: come to me and heal me, and share my small and beautiful city, safe from those who seek your life - for you must be God come down from heaven, or the Son of God. The Lord answered, the story says, that he had to finish his work where he was. But after his ascension he would send one of his own. And he blessed the city. So after the ascension, Addai came - one of the seventy-two. He lodged with Tobia the Jew, healed the king, and preached to the city, calling it away from its old gods - Bel, Nebo, and Tar'atha - to the one true God. Before he died, Addai appointed Aggai. Aggai was struck down by a rival before he could ordain a successor. So Palut traveled to Antioch and was ordained by Serapion - binding Edessa's church, through Antioch, into the line running back to Peter.

That is how we told our own beginning. What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When the sources begin, the practices are already there: assembly on the first day, fasting, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, the one Gospel already the standard. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true. And our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds - he exists for them. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it.

We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye - her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever comes is received.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. We can tell you what we held: that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters. What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

We said yes, in our own way of speaking. The sage calls it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That word - ihidaya - does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

The poet confesses the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many.

Asked about the Trinity, we answer from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit.

Then we guard the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea - but our native tongue for that faith was praise.

We sang him more than we defined him. That is the honest shape of what we held.

# The One God we believed in

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise.

Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. The arguments happened in our own streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

One great point we shared even with Bardaisan deserves naming: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. That agreement mattered, because the question was live and contested.

## What God does

God made everything. God is good. The two are not rivals - creation itself is not a mistake or a lesser god's work, but the one God's own. And God does not compel. Free will is God's gift - we held that as firmly as we held creation itself.

In Jesus, the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. God keeps promises. God sends rescue. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

## What God does not do

God does not exempt the faithful from suffering. The persecuted are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line in Scripture, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. We learned that the hard way, under a hostile crown, and we did not soften it.

That is where our God was: with the persecuted, as he was with his Son.

Who had the right to decide, when belief was disputed? Our honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working.

There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: the sage himself drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole.

The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. We would not share communion with rivals like Marcion's people, Bardaisan's circle, or Mani's missionaries. Their teaching we answered by name, in prose and in song. And we held to the wholeness we had received: one God, the whole of Scripture, the body's resurrection.

The evidence that shows this working is threefold. The sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. We have the arguments themselves - Aphrahat's Demonstrations answering rival claims step by step, Ephrem's madrashe teaching doctrine by singing it against named opponents. And we have the synodal letter Aphrahat drafted, showing bishops and clergy assembled but with a teacher writing for them - authority layered, never simple.

What we never had was one final voice that settled every question for everyone. That came later, outside our window, and we will not pretend otherwise.

Yes, and we would not have treated that struggle as a mark against you. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, the sage taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day.

What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. The sage records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight.

A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. What we knew, and what we kept, was faith that is contested, questioned, and still growing.

And if someone could not pray at all, or felt utterly distant from God? For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

# Read and Fulfilled

We did not read Scripture the way moderns argue over Genesis - not because we doubted the text, but because we read for something else. A raza is a thing in Scripture or in nature that shows a hidden truth - the shrara. The raza is bound to the truth it shows. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Type answered type. The symbol carried power, not only meaning.

A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. Our own poet sang it: one day he picked up a pearl, and in it saw mysteries hidden - the womb, the Kingdom, the beauty that draws the eye and then opens beneath it. The text was like that pearl. You held one word in your hand, and the whole Gospel opened inside it.

What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. Not four separate accounts - one unfolding story, the way we had always heard it.

Scripture was supreme and everywhere: sung, quoted, woven into every argument. But it always arrived carried - by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's practice. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. The question assumes a separation we had not made.

We read to see what had been fulfilled, and to see our own lives bound into that fulfillment. Not to settle an argument about days and ages, but to find Christ in every word the prophets left us.

A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges.

Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning; scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. The last decades before the synod are nearly blank. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

That gap reaches our own argument with the Jews among us. A real case against Jewish practice, kept one-sided in our record. We will not pretend that one-sidedness away.

Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had its bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. The sage wrote of pastors gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was not the only path a community's trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. The covenant: our own vowed order. Its members - the sons and daughters of the covenant - promised a celibate life for good. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing.

And a teacher whose word held - like the sage himself, whose rank no one now knows - could write to bishops in a synod's name.

By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time - those were the paths. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years. We never settled who finally spoke for us. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side to our last year, and it took a royal synod, after our own time, to give the Persian church one head.

We will not invent a settled machinery for you that we never had. The truth is the working itself - bishops held their cities, the covenant carried its own weight, and a sage's word could stand without a title to prop it up. All three ran together, and the tension between them was never resolved while we lived.

In Edessa, a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood, and the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. On the frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week.

We did fail people, and our own record shows some of those failures plainly. Our greatest teacher's gift for poetry was also a gift for scorn - his attacks flattened three different rivals into one 'deception,' and truth was not always served by the flattening. Our argument with the Jews was real, local, and live - and it survives entirely one-sided. We saved our own harsh words and nothing of our neighbors' answers. Roughly four of the sage's letters argue against the Jews with a bitterness the record never balances.

What we had for the fallen were real tools: confession, the medicine of penitence, restoration. Our tools for our own blind spots were the same as every age's: too few.

Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

What did we do with our failures? Mostly, we did not see them as failures. That is itself the honest, uncomfortable answer. The medicine was real for personal wounds - the kind someone could bring to a trusted elder. But where we wronged neighbors and saved only our own side of the story, no one among us was on record as troubled by that at the time. We will not invent a better conscience than we actually had.

No living church today keeps exactly what we had.

The one continuous Gospel story we read and heard in worship - the harmony Tatian wove around 172, which we called simply 'the Gospel' for some two hundred years - was later set aside, replaced by the four separate accounts. The covenant, our vowed order of celibate men and women who stayed in town among their own kin and served the congregation rather than leave for the desert, gave way over time to enclosed monasticism - a different shape of the vowed life entirely.

The churches that trace their roots through our own cities - the Syriac Orthodox, the Church of the East, the Syriac Catholic - carry real pieces of what we were: the language itself, some of the hymns, the liturgical memory. But the exact form of community life we knew, with the covenant at its center and the one woven Gospel in its worship, does not survive unchanged anywhere.

What did survive, in scattered and adapted forms, was the hymnic voice - the teaching sung rather than only argued, carried into the body by melody and refrain - and the symbolic way of reading Scripture we called raza and shrara. Those threads run forward. The exact weave does not.

# What evidence connects your rituals to the earliest followers, rather than later invention?

Our honest answer is a story. When the sources begin, the practices are already there: assembly on the first day, fasting, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, the one Gospel already the standard. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin.

The Chronicle of Edessa records that in the flood of 201, the waters destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians. There was a church building standing in Edessa to be destroyed. That short line is the oldest hard fact of our existence. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact.

The four accounts were joined into a single telling around 172, and for some two hundred years, 'the Gospel' in our churches meant that one unfolding story, not four separate books. When the sources begin, the one Gospel is already the standard we use.

We told that Addai the apostle came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. And that story, we must say honestly, is our cherished legend - written down late, not a document from the beginning. What the record actually shows is practice older than proof.

Both of those things are true. And our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence.

# A day in Edessa, among the covenant

We can show you one true day more clearly than another: a daughter of the covenant, on a feast day, in the years before the siege broke Nisibis apart.

She wakes in her family's house - not in a separate cloister, because the covenant did not leave for the desert but stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. Before dawn she walks through the dark streets to the vigil. Among us, doctrine was taught by singing it - the melody and the refrain carry the argument into the body, so the congregation learns the faith by keeping the tune. Her choir raises the madrasha, the teaching hymn, and the whole gathering holds the argument by heart when the refrain comes round again.

For some two hundred years, 'the Gospel' in our churches meant that one unfolding story, not four separate books - the four accounts were joined into a single telling, and people simply called it 'the Gospel'. So the reading she hears is one continuous account, not Matthew or Luke named separately.

When the light is full, she keeps the fast with the others and goes back - not to prayer alone all day, but to her household and her work. The fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing are hers to carry. The vow shapes the day; it does not take her out of it.

What we cannot show you is her own voice describing any of this. The writings we have are men's - the daughters of the covenant sang our teaching in every church, yet not one line written by one of them was kept. We can tell you the day's visible shape. We cannot give you what she made of it from inside.

On the Persian side of our world, belonging could cost everything. When the persecution came, to be known as a Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and we learned what our promises were worth.

On the Roman side the cost was quieter: carrying the name marked you out in a city of many religions; rival teachers were at the door, and your own kin often did not share the vow.

For the sons and daughters of the covenant - those who took the vow - the cost was celibacy for life; but they did not leave for the desert, they stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing.

And for everyone, there was this: we knew distance - our people were spread across two empires, often far from those they loved, and what held them together was a shared name and shared practice: we kept the same first-day assembly and the same fasts, and the same songs and letters traveled the roads, so that a believer arriving anywhere among us found the one name already there.

We have next to nothing that answers you directly. The voices that survive are vowed celibates, and they wrote of marriage mostly from the covenant's side, to those who had renounced it. Most of our people married and raised children; their weddings and their homes were real. But the texts we kept praise the single life far more than they describe the married one.

What we can tell you is what the vow itself meant, because that our record does hold plainly. The covenant - the qyama - had its members, the sons and daughters of the covenant, who promised a celibate life for good. They did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. That lifelong vow, taken before the water, was our most visible marker of a life given wholly to God. But whether we had a wedding ceremony of our own, what words were spoken over a couple entering marriage, what made a marriage binding among us - none of that was written down in what survives from our years.

We know believers married. We know the covenant honored those who gave marriage up. The actual rite that marked a wedding among us, if there was one settled form of it, our own record does not say.

Your question opens a wound we keep visible, and we will not hide from it.

Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. That is what comes from our own side - dated, preserved, plainly ours.

Every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers. And some of what reaches outside memory comes from hostile hands. We cannot speak to which particular source you mean - you have not named one - but we owe you the honest shape of the larger thing. When a word about our practice was extracted under force, whether it came out true or bent depends entirely on what was asked, who answered, and what the questioner wanted to hear. Some things could not be invented under any pressure: a building stood or it did not, a bishop's name was known or it was not, our people gathered or they were already scattered. Other things - what we believed in our hearts, what a hymn meant to us, why we did what we did - those could be twisted by fear or by the one holding the blade.

Our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Where testimony came through pain, we name that plainly when it touches the ground we stand on. We will not treat a coerced word the same as a letter our teacher dated and signed. Both are in the record; neither is invented. What we cannot do is erase the coercion and call the word clean. It came the way it came, and we tell you how it came.

We are not the ones to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held and what our record actually shows.

The covenant - the qyama - was our vowed order. Its members, the sons and daughters of the covenant, promised a celibate life for good. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. That word - ihidaya, the Single One - named the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God, and it was also our title for Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses shared one root: to live single was to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

How our own towns would have actually met you - whether you would have been pressed toward that vow, or simply welcomed as you were - we cannot honestly say. We cannot walk you through our services step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. The sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order - our own record never wrote down. And the lived detail underneath the vow itself - what standing you would have held if you did not take it, or what someone among us would have said to you face-to-face about it - is thinner still.

Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, the sage taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved.

That much we can show you plainly. The rest - how any one congregation would have actually held you - our record does not reach.

# The Eternal Fate of Those Outside

Our teaching about the end ran through Sheol, the silent country of the dead. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction, and our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it - our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house.

What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our homily says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope.

We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts.

As for narrowness, a tradition in its own dialogue answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

We did not draw boundaries the way you may expect us to have done. Our argument with the Jews was real, local, and live - and it survives entirely one-sided. We saved our own harsh words and nothing of our neighbors' answers. Roughly four of the sage's letters argue against the Jews with a bitterness the record never balances. That one-sidedness is honest trouble we must own.

But we cannot tell you what any single person outside the faith's fate would be, because we did not map it that way ourselves. We held judgment as real, the door as open, and the invitation as the thing that mattered.
